newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong spends last day under British rule.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong spends last day under British rule.

text.p: Hong Kong began its last day under Britain's rule on Monday amid the conflicting emotions of elation over reunion with China and concern over its future freedoms.
With most people enjoying five days of public holidays to mark Hong Kong's return to China, the mood in the territory has been relaxed.

Office towers on either side of Victoria Harbour glowed at night with messages commemorating the transition. Scores of parties and celebrations were set to run alongside the official ceremonies, parades and fireworks displays.

British Prime Minister Tony Blair's busy day begins at midday and ends just after the midnight (1600 GMT) ceremony to end 156 years of British rule. In between, he will meet Chinese President Jiang Zemin. and Chris Patten, Hong Kong's 28th and last colonial governor.

Jiang, who will be presented with Britain's last major territory by heir to the throne Prince Charles, vowed in Beijing on Sunday to fulfil the promises made by China under the 1984 Sino-British pact on the handover.

"We will firmly uphold the principles of 'one country, two systems' and 'Hong Kong people governing Hong Kong' as well as a high degree of autonomy," Jiang said at a ceremony in the Great Hall of the People.
China will "safeguard the Hong Kong residents' rights and freedoms in accordance with the law," the official Xinhua news agency quoted him as saying.

Security was tight around a waterfront hotel owned by billionaire Li Ka-shing where Jiang and Premier Li Peng were expected to stay. A heavy security cordon was also in place around the Convention Centre where 4,000 VIPs will attend a gala banquet before witnessing the handover ceremony.

Members of the Black Watch and the last of Britain's other forces in Hong Kong will hold a farewell parade at sunset before flying out by the early hours of July 1 when Prince Charles and Patten leave aboard the royal yacht Britannia.

The United States criticised China for its decision to send in 4,000 troops by armoured car, helicopter and warship within hours of the handover. "I don't think this is the best way to start off," visiting U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said.

Tung Chee-hwa, the shipping magnate chosen by Beijing to take the helm in Hong Kong, told Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer that elections for a new legislature would be held next May, Downer said on Sunday.
Tung had earlier promised a vote within a year but had not named the month.

A democratically-elected Legislative Council, Britain's parting political gift to Hong Kong and the focus of bitter Sino-British feuding, is being scrapped in favour of a provisional legislature approved by Beijing.
Andrew Cheng, an elected member of the Legislative Council, heaped scorn on Tung's promise of May elections.

"It's a beautiful lie," he said as a small group of pro-democracy activists erected banners outside the Convention Centre condemning the provisional legislature and calling on China to free jailed dissidents.

British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook vowed to defend the democratic legacy. "The people of Hong Kong have now had a taste of democracy. It must be a prime objective of British policy to make sure that taste does not become a memory," he told reporters.
Pro-democracy activists and legislators say they will protest outside the Convention Centre and hold a vigil at the Legislative Council building in the hours straddling the handover.
They have been warned against staging a planned protest on the building's balcony while Beijing-appointed lawmakers are sworn in down the road early on July 1.
Under controversial laws prepared by the new legislature and due to come into force retroactively at midnight, police approval will be needed for demonstrations.
Patten attacked "demeaning, patronising, mule-headed" arguments against democracy in the territory, whose new leaders have stressed stability ahead of individual freedoms.
He lambasted a "small band of self-appointed good-mouthers who tell the world that Hong Kongers don't care about democracy and civil liberties but only about making money."
